Reticence is the quality of being unwilling to speak freely or share information. It is the tendency to hold back your thoughts, feelings, or knowledge — to say less than you could, especially about things that are personal or sensitive.

Think of it this way: imagine a person who has lived through something significant, but when asked about it, they give short answers, change the subject, or stay quiet. That holding-back quality they have — that is reticence.

Reticence is not just silence. A reticent person can speak — they simply choose not to say much, particularly about certain things. The word points to a restraint in communication, a drawing inward of one's words.

It can describe:

  • A person's general nature — someone who is habitually quiet and private by personality.
  • A person's behavior in a specific situation — someone who is normally open, but becomes tight-lipped when a particular topic comes up.

"Despite hours of questioning, his reticence never cracked — he revealed almost nothing."

"There was a careful reticence about her that made people feel she always knew more than she was saying."
What Reticence Is NOT — Important Distinctions

Because reticence is easily confused with similar words, understanding what makes it different is crucial to truly owning its meaning.

Reticence vs. Silence
Silence is simply not speaking. Reticence is the quality or habit of holding back. You can be silent for one moment. But reticence is something deeper — a characteristic or tendency. A reticent person has a pattern of restraint.

Reticence vs. Shyness
A shy person wants to speak but feels uncomfortable, anxious, or afraid to do so. Shyness is rooted in social discomfort. Reticence is rooted in unwillingness to disclose — it is a conscious or deeply habitual choice to keep things in. A reticent person may be perfectly comfortable in social situations; they simply don't volunteer much about themselves.

Reticence vs. Secretiveness
Secretiveness implies actively hiding something, often with a sense of scheming or deception. Reticence is more passive and dignified — it is simply not offering information, not necessarily concealing it with bad intent.

Reticence vs. Taciturnity
Taciturnity means being generally very quiet and speaking very little across all topics, almost as a permanent state. Reticence is more flexible — a person can be reticent about specific things while being quite talkative about others.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

Reticence carries a neutral to slightly admirable tone. When you call someone reticent, you are not necessarily criticizing them. In many cultures, reticence is associated with dignity, discretion, wisdom, and self-control. It suggests someone who thinks before speaking and does not overshare.

However, depending on context, reticence can also feel frustrating — especially if someone's holding back is getting in the way of honest communication.

A diplomat's reticence is a skill. A friend's reticence when you need them to open up can feel like a wall.

The word itself has a slightly formal, literary feel, which is why it often appears in writing about politics, psychology, relationships, and character descriptions.

As a noun, reticence is used in these common patterns:

With "about" or "on" — to point to what someone is unwilling to discuss:

"Her reticence about her finances made it hard to help her."
"His reticence on the subject of his family was well known."

As a general quality of a person:

"She was admired for her reticence — she never spread gossip."
"His reticence was legendary; you could never get a straight answer out of him."

With "show," "display," or "characteristic of":

"He showed a certain reticence when the conversation turned personal."
"Her reticence was characteristic of someone who had learned, through pain, to keep quiet."
A Disputed Modern Use — Know This

In modern usage, you will sometimes encounter "reticence" used to mean reluctance to do something in a broader sense, not just reluctance to speak:

"The committee showed reticence to approve the funding."

Traditionalists — and most careful writers — consider this incorrect. In its precise, classical meaning, reticence specifically refers to reluctance to speak or reveal information, not reluctance to act in general. The correct word for that broader meaning is simply "reluctance."

So: if you want to be precise and correct, use reticence only when the holding-back is about speech and disclosure. Use "reluctance" when it is about action in general. Knowing this distinction immediately puts you ahead of many native speakers.
The One-Sentence Summary to Lock It In

Reticence is the quality of being unwilling to speak freely or share personal information — a calm, deliberate restraint in what you reveal through words.

If you remember one image: picture a person who listens a great deal, speaks carefully and sparingly, and never says more than they mean to — that person embodies reticence.
